What is the disposition of moneys payable by the government to persons confined to a hospital for the chronically ill who are in receipt of (a) old age security (b) old age assistance (c) blind persons allowances under the Blind Persons Act (d) disabled persons allowances under the Disabled Persons Act; and what is the reason for the difference in the disposition of the moneys?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
(a) Pensions under the Old Age Security Act are payable as of right to persons 70 years of age and over who fulfil the requirements of the act and the regulations made under it. There is no means test attached to these pensions. The administration of the Old Age Security Act is a federal responsibility. Pensions are payable to pensioners in chronic hospitals and the pensioners are free to dispose of their pensions as with any other asset. The exception is where a pensioner is declared to be incapable of managing his own affairs in which case the director of old age security appoints a trustee to administer the pension on behalf of the pensioner, (b) Old age assistance, blind persons allowances and (c) disabled persons allowances are paid and administered; (d) by provincial authorities under the authority of provincial acts. In accordance with the terms of agreements made by the government of Canada with the provinces under the authority of the Old Age Assistance Act, the Blind Persons Act and the Disabled Persons Act, the provinces may claim reimbursement by the government of Canada of 50 per cent of their expenditure for old age assistance and disabled persons allowances and 75 per cent of their expenditure for blind persons allowances.
The decision as to the payment of old age assistance, blind persons allowance or disabled persons allowance to a person in a chronic hospital or to any other person is a provincial responsibility. However in order for a province to obtain the federal share its decisions authorizing the payment of assistance or allowances must be in accordance with the terms of the agreements referred to above.
Any difference between payments to pensioners under the Old Age Security Act and

Questions
to recipients of old age assistance, blind persons allowances or disabled persons allowances in chronic hospitals, or any difference between benefits paid by a particular province under the three programs it administers to persons in chronic hospitals, would be explained partly by the fact that income is not a factor in determining the eligibility of an applicant for old age security and partly by specific provisions in federal legislation dealing with institutions and provincial policy decisions.

speechtext:
1.	In the provinces, where the R.C.M.P. is under provincial contract, how does the work divide as between federal, provincial, and municipal duties?
2.	Is the man strength provided under the provincial contract sufficient to take care of the work that the contract imposes in the cases of Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, and British Columbia?
3.	Is any formula currently in operation to ensure an approximately equal work load per member of the force in the aforementioned contract provinces?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: WORK OF R.C.M.P. UNDER PROVINCIAL CONTRACTS
speechtext:
1. In the
provinces where the R.C.M. police is under contract a stipulated number of men are employed under the terms of the contract to carry out provincial duties, and likewise an agreed upon number of men are employed under each municipal contract to perform duties within the confines of the municipal area. In addition, the R.C.M. police maintain in each province a number of men who are considered adequate to carry out federal duties.
2.	The man strength provided under the provincial contracts is under constant review with the provincial authorities and under normal conditions is sufficient to take care of the work load. There have been occasions where-due to unusual circumstances developing-as, for example, Doukhobor depredations in British Columbia-it has been necessary to reinforce the divisions during the period of such emergency.
3.	The R.C.M. police operates under a manpower establishment. One of the primary purposes of this system is to provide for the

proper distribution of the strength of the force in each province to take care of the work load in any particular area.

1.	Does the government plan to tie in the construction of new armouries with civil defence?
2.	Has the government any plans to construct new armouries underground?

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United Nations general assembly has now concluded its discussion of the question of race conflict in South Africa resulting from the policies of apartheid, with which was linked the question of the treatment of people of Indian and Indo-Pakistani origin. The resolution, sponsored by 33 African and Asian members, was passed yesterday in a plenary session of the general assembly by 67 votes in favour to 16 opposed, with 23 abstentions.
The resolution deplores the failure of the South African government to comply with repeated requests and demands of the United Nations to abandon its racial policies and requests members, separately or collectively, to undertake specific diplomatic and economic sanctions against South Africa. The resolution also establishes a special committee to be nominated by the president of the assembly to keep the racial policies of South Africa under review, and invites member states to inform the next session of the assembly of actions they have taken to dissuade the government of South Africa from pursuing its apartheid policies. Finally, the resolution requests the security council to take appropriate measures, including sanctions, to secure South Africa's compliance with assembly resolutions on this subject and to consider South Africa's expulsion from the United Nations.
The hon. member for Queens, my parliamentary secretary, made it clear in his statement on this subject before the special committee of the assembly that Canada condemns without any qualification the South African government's harsh and repressive policy of apartheid. The Canadian delegation, while strongly supporting the aims of the resolution, voted against it as a whole because of our grave doubts about the appropriateness of the use of sanctions by the United Nations in a situation which does not involve external aggression or a question of peace or war. We are also opposed to the expulsion

of South Africa from the United Nations because of the principle involved and because the United Nations has more opportunity to exert its influence with South Africa in the organization.
No opportunity was given to vote clause by clause because a resolution was put through by a very small majority providing that the only vote could be on the resolution as a whole. Canada, for example, would have voted in favour of the clause calling for the setting up of a committee.
With regard to action Canada will take, may I say this. The hon. member will notice that the resolution requests the security council to take the next step. Until any such further step is taken it would be premature for me to make any statement on the Canadian position.

I have a supplementary question. In view of the action taken by the Prime Minister of Canada at the second last conference of prime ministers which led to the expulsion of South Africa from the commonwealth, does the minister not think he owes to the house and the country a more precise and comprehensive explanation for not voting for this resolution at the United Nations?

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when we rose at ten o'clock on Thursday evening I had been answering a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture to the effect that under the policy of the government small farmers could get their required funds from banks through the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act. I want to demonstrate very briefly that the small farmers, under this government, have been very seriously discriminated against in obtaining credit from the Farm Credit Corporation.
The minister was kind enough to provide me with a table of loans of various sizes provided by the Farm Credit Corporation. I do not want to burden the house with a lot of detail but this table shows that eight loans under $2,000 were provided in the year ended March 31, 1961, and in the following year ended March 31, 1962, these had been reduced to one. In the number of loans from $2,000 to $3,000 there had been a reduction of 41, from 72 to 31; loans of $3,000 to $4,000, a reduction of 62, from 176 to 114; loans of $4,000 to $5,000, a reduction of 87, from 292 to 205; loans of $5,000 to $6,000, a reduction of 69, from 391 to 322; loans of $6,000 to $7,000, a reduction of 64, from 462 to 398; loans of $7,000 to $8,000, a reduction of 49, from 503 to 454, and in loans of $8,000 to $9,000, a reduction of 14, from 470 to 456.
In the categories of loans below $9,000 there was a reduction of 405 in the total number

of loans. It is true there was an increase in the over-all number of loans by some 288, but if you take the $9,000 loan as the breaking point, then below $9,000 there were 405 fewer loans and above $9,000 there were 693 additional loans. This is very clear evidence that the Farm Credit Corporation is moving in the wrong direction, namely to choke off the number of loans to small farmers. I am not complaining about the number of larger loans provided, but when that number is increased the number of smaller loans should also be increased.
If a farmer comes in seeking a $3,000 loan the minister says "Let him use the Farm Improvement Loans Act; let him go to the banks", but the minister knows it is not possible for any farmer to get a loan from the banks, under the provisions of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, to purchase land. On the other hand 59 per cent of the money supplied by the Farm Credit Corporation has been used for land purchases; 22 per cent has gone to pay existing obligations against land and, over all, 80 per cent has been used in connection with the purchasing of new land and consolidating mortgages against land already purchased.
In other words, 80 per cent of the money provided by the Farm Credit Corporation is devoted to land purchases and the small farmers cannot get money for land purchases when they go to the banks. When they want to buy additional land they must come to the Farm Credit Corporation and that corporation is turning them down.
I suggest that the government should not continue closing the doors to small farmers seeking credit. The small farmer who can improve his position by buying additional land should be encouraged and should be provided with this kind of credit.
The expansion of the total aggregate provided for by this legislation is good. In fact it should be expanded even more and we say that the small farmer should be given a chance and that the minister should not say "Let him go to the banks" when the banks are unable, under the terms of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, to provide money for the purchase of land. We suggest there should be a much greater emphasis placed on providing money for the small farmer, and the government and the corporation should stop closing the doors in his face.

Mr. Chairman, in connection with the proposed legislation under the Farm Credit Act, very briefly I should like to direct the attention of the minister to two aspects of the act and its administration which bring about some measure of unfairness. The first has to do with policy, and the second with administration. I think the minister is well aware that there are areas of eastern Canada, particularly in Ontario, where the lending authority of the corporation is not geared to meet local conditions. The Niagara peninsula, the counties of Norfolk, Elgin, Kent and Essex, I think provide excellent examples. Climate, topography and the fertility of the soil have combined to give this area a high value for its land. The land, in fact, is more highly valued than lands in many other parts of Canada.
Since I have a more intimate knowledge of the county of Kent, it would perhaps be more authoritative to draw on examples in that particular county. I would emphasize that I am informed the same situation exists in other areas. The cost of land in Kent, land which is improved, tiled and equipped with adequate dwelling and outbuildings, varies between $250 and $500 per acre, and the minimum acreages that are recognized as efficient farm units vary from 150 to 250, depending on the crops that are grown. The more costly lands are farmed more intensively and can operate efficiently in units of 150 acres. Lands which sell at $250 an acre are considered efficient units in 250 acre parcels. It follows, therefore, that land costs for efficient farm units vary from $60,000 to $75,000, and the cost of suitable equipment varies between $12,000 and $15,000.
I think it will readily be seen that part II loans on the land maximum are limited in effect to 30 per cent of the value of the land, and part III loans are in approximately the same relationship. The net effect of the present policy of the corporation is to lend to approximately 30 per cent of the value of land in Kent and similarly situate areas, and 60 per cent of value in the remainder of Canada. This unfairness, Mr. Chairman, is magnified even further because the size of the loans required in this particular area pretty well rule out private lenders; that source of fixed capital is not readily available. As a matter of fact, they would much prefer to invest in government bonds at the attractive interest rates. Also, corporate loans which were available in the past to farmers in that area are no longer available because of the competition which has been offered by the Farm Credit Corporation. Farmers, there-

Farm Credit Act
fore, find themselves in the position that private loans are not available, corporate loans are not readily available, and yet they are limited by this ceiling to $20,000 which, with great respect, is not adequate having regard to the figures I have indicated as to the value of the land.
Therefore I would respectfully suggest to the minister that there be an upward revision of the ceiling on these loans. I quite agree that the basis of 60 per cent of value should remain, and I think that is probably one of the reasons the percentage of losses by the corporation has been one of which we can well be proud. However, it seems to me it is most desirable that all farmers everywhere should be in the position where they are able to borrow on an equitable and rateable basis. This can only be done, having regard to the value of the lands in the areas of which I speak, if the ceilling of $20,000 and $27,500 under the two portions of the act is raised. I would respectfully suggest that this inequity should be corrected, and I believe it would be in keeping with the intention of the act at the time the scope of operations of this corporation was extended.
The second matter to which I should like to direct the minister's attention involves administration. I believe it also deserves immediate attention. I can supply to the minister particulars of a loan transaction which was needlessly delayed for six months. The loan application was made with the co-operation of the local office of the corporation; the inspection was made in the normal course, and reported promptly; the loan was approved by the corporation in good time and the legal branch at the Ontario office completed its work quickly, or reasonably quickly. There then followed six months delay before the closing of that transaction. I suggest to the minister that this is a most undesirable situation. It is most undesirable because all the employees of the corporation, as well as his own department, are subjected to criticism, unjust criticism, for conduct that is totally unnecessary. The policy of selecting local solicitors to carry out part of the functions of the corporation in local areas is not one which I am prepared to suggest should be changed. I must recognize that there are some qualified solicitors in the county of Kent who either through environmental influences or otherwise have not yet seen the light and are probably able to qualify to serve the corporation.
It would be my suggestion, Mr. Chairman, notwithstanding the fact that more recent developments have, I believe, indicated a 16-day check-up in connection with routine work through these offices, that it would be most desirable that steps be taken to appoint two

or three or more agents in local areas in order that this work might proceed quickly. Very often it transpires that this work is assigned to one office, a busy office which apparently prefers to do the normal work of private clients first, and the work of the commission receives secondary consideration.
May I close by saying that if in anything I have said I have reflected unfavourably on the commission's employees or on the routine or procedure which it follows, I should like to correct this. It has been my experience that this corporation is working efficiently and is subject to the delays which occur normally during the winter when an inspection is not possible. I believe that this work is being done effectively, and I very much regret that criticism is advanced against employees of the commission and the commission itself because of this one shortcoming.

Mr. Chairman, we import more than 20 million poultry for consumption purposes only, while we have in this country a great number of poultry farmers who would be only too glad to increase their production and thus help check unemployment in Canada. But they do not have the financial means to do so, they do not have the necessary capital to build new hen houses, neither to buy in great quantity the feed grain which they would need. Finally, they do not have the necessary capital to buy in great quantity the chicks they would like to raise and feed.
Their only solution at present is to be financed by a grain company which, in doing so, can count on a constant and non-competitive market for its products, or else by a chain store company which can thus count on a constant supply of chickens at a relatively low price. In both cases, the poultry farmers are losing completely the control

of their business and are becoming, to all intents and purposes, salaried workers in their own business. Neither the grain companies nor the chain store companies will finance poultry farmers with a view to help them; they will simply do so because of a financial advantage. Besides, how could we blame them, any more than the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) has blamed the companies which are financing his car sales.
Grain companies, like those finance companies of the hon. member for Villeneuve, will finance a business or a sale only with a view to making a profit. But, meanwhile, our poultry farmers are getting discouraged and wilfully abandon poultry farming, when they are not simply put out of business. In my constituency only, that of Argenteuil-Deux-Montagnes, there are at least about 50 poultry farms which used to be very prosperous and which are now completely abandoned.
And yet, we have imported from the United States, in the last fiscal year, more than 20 million birds for consumption purposes.
Is there a solution to that problem? I see a double solution. First, loans should be granted to our poultry farmers, as loans are granted to other farmers, because is it not true that poultry farming is also part of agriculture?
On the other hand, it seems to me that the government could put a stop to that real dumping from our neighbours to the south in our country, because we know that through its austerity program the government succeeded in putting a stop or in making more difficult the importation of goods we cannot produce here and that we must import. Therefore we are justified in wondering if this same government could not put an embargo on the importation of poultry, in order to help our poultry farmers who certainly have not been spoiled in the last five years.
To come back to the financing of farm loans, I would ask the Minister of Agriculture to give us some details on the amendments he made or intends to make concerning the rules of the corporation which those in charge of farm loans have to carry out. The minister told us that henceforth the value of a poultry operation would be taken into account in the assessment and the appraisal of the economical soundness of a farm. Unless I am mistaken, he added however that the corporation had no intention of financing units exclusively devoted to poultry farming. Could the minister give us more details in that regard and tell us what will be the proportion of loans granted to poultry farms by the Farm Credit Corporation?
Farm Credit Act
It is imperative that credit be made available to our farmers who operate a poultry farm in order to take advantage of the local market at least.

When that seed is exported to the United States its productive capacity is enormous in a softer climate, and we are not capitalizing enough on our northern grown seed. It is highly viable and of tremendous value principally because it is disease free in the cold climatic conditions under which it grows.
Many of the diseases in seed crops and clover crops are carried by insects, largely aphids, I think they are called vectors, which carry the disease from one plant to another. In an extremely cold climate there are no aphids and the result is that we get a seed of fantastic value as compared with seed from other countries.
I would like to see a special standard set for Canadian seed grown above a certain northern latitude and I am quite certain that if we adhere to that standard we would export even more seed than we do at present. No. 3: is there any agency in Newfoundland to which a small farmer may apply for a loan under this act or for advice as to eligibility for a loan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR INCREASE IN LENDING CAPACITY
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there is no limit on size; it is a question of whether it is an economic unit. Yes, they can borrow for fencing and reclaiming land; but, once again, it is for the purpose of making it a more economic unit. There is no office at the present time in Newfoundland; the closest office is at Moncton.

Mr. Chairman, I want to support the remarks of the hon. member for Rosthern with regard to the desirability of changing the phrase "an economic unit" to "a more economic unit". However, I can see some great advantages in having the word "more" inserted before "economic unit". I think this would be a most important change. I think this is the kind of change we often make in committee in the normal course of dealing with a measure of this kind. on this side. I am, therefore, Mr. Chairman, going to move an amendment to this clause. I move:
That clause 2 be amended by adding the following :

I would ask the minister to give this matter his consideration. There may be some arguments for and against. The minister said that if he was a lawyer, he would say so-and-so. Neither am I a lawyer. I think he might give this matter his further mature consideration, and I would hope that when this amendment is put to the committee it would receive the unanimous approval of the committee. I do not propose to embark on a long speech in order to demonstrate the truth of what I am saying, because I am firmly convinced that no farsighted Canadian can oppose such a measure. That is why logic and common sense proclaim that we must, as from now, have our national anthem.

National Anthem
attended by Canadians of both language groups. My immediate neighbours were English speaking Canadians. When the time came for the singing of the national anthem, I was happily surprised to hear them sing the "O Canada" in English, as fervently as I was doing in French. 1 realized then that it was possible for English speaking and French speaking Canadians to work together for a greater Canada, in a true spirit of national unity. Indeed, whenever I hear "O Canada" being played on the carillon of the peace tower, I am deeply moved because it is the most beautiful anthem in the world. The well-known writer and musician, Eugene Lapierre, said this, one day:
As it often happens with great writers and musicians, it is a childhood souvenir which inspired the writing of such a masterpiece as "O Canada". A small waterfall was the source of inspiration for a lyrical and solemn march which is so beautiful that the first notes B-D-G sound like Mozart's "Magic Flute". The very first bars reach the musical heights of Canadian nature. The march of a people becomes a fugue in which all the battalions in history pass before one's eyes as is so well illustrated by this inspired verse of this sublime musical poem: "Thy history is an epic of the most dazzling deeds".
Therefore, the anthem "O Canada" is a chant, a hymn to the glory of our forefathers and of our country, which should make us prouder and happier to be Canadians. In consequence, I humbly request the hon. members of the house to refrain from speaking on this motion so as not to kill the project.
Let us show our good will through an act of sacrifice, and to this end, I suggest that the question be put immediately for the recognition of "O Canada" as the distinctive national anthem of our country, as it exists at present in its French version and according to an English version which would be chosen by the government.

Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the request just made by the hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote), I think it is proper for someone from another party to add a few words on this motion, just a few words, in order not to be held responsible if the motion is not put to a vote today.
In October 1956, I was invited by Senator Thorvaldson, to a football game in Winnipeg, and I must say I was quite surprised when, arriving on the field, we heard the organ playing the first bars of "O Canada" and we saw a crowd of about 20,000 rise and sing our national anthem, and this in a part of Canada which is considered as rather English, while

here in Ottawa, in Toronto, in Hamilton, people were singing "God Save the Queen" and dared to call it the national anthem.

That is wrong.

And since then, we have seen students from Barrie, Ontario, rise in protest, not against "God Save the Queen", but against the fact that "God Save the Queen" was being referred to as our national anthem. They are right on that point.
I have always rebelled somewhat on hearing the announcement before a football game or a hockey game or any other event: "Our national anthem" and then hearing "God Save the Queen".
A national anthem is an anthem which is peculiar to one country only. The "Marseillaise" is not sung in countries other than France; the American anthem is not sung elsewhere than in the United States. A national anthem must be a country's own anthem and "God Save the Queen" is not proper to Canada. It is an anthem which is sung in all parts of the commonwealth. It is rather a royal anthem which we like to sing on certain occasions, a royal anthem which is perhaps sung too often here in Canada without the protocol observed in England.
In England as a matter of fact when the Queen is not present they only play the first bars of "God Save the Queen." But here, whether the Governor General is present or not, it is played in its entirety. Is it that we have become more English than the English themselves?
Some time ago, I received letters about my intervention in a previous debate on the matter. I have here a letter from someone of Ottawa who congratulates me for having asked for a national anthem other than "God Save the Queen". with warmth and devotion, because she is Canada's sovereign. But when it comes to a national anthem, the only anthem is "O Canada", because it seems to be accepted by almost everybody in Canada.
A few years ago a survey was made in the schools-the English high schools in Canada-among the students of 18, 19 and 20 years of age, and 48 per cent said they were in favour of "O Canada", while 17 per cent were against it and the remainder had no opinion. This shows that the idea of having "O Canada" as our national anthem is spreading constantly.
I realize that some people do not like the English version. It does not seem so bad to me:

Since the treaty of Westminster, Canada is on an equal basis with Britain and the other members of the commonwealth. We do not have to accept what comes from abroad, no more than "La Marseillaise" should be sung in Quebec or elsewhere in the country as the national anthem of Canada.
I have heard it said in this house that the music of "O Canada" was not beautiful, that Calixa Lavallee's composition was poor.

Mr. Speaker, I will not detain the house for long. However, I wish to express our warm agreement with and acceptance of the excellent resolution introduced by the hon. member for
National Anthem
Chicoutimi (Mr. Cote). I am particularly happy to do so when I recognize the source from which the resolution comes. We believe that Canada should have a distinctive national anthem and a distinctive national flag. We believe that the hon. member has made the most appropriate selection possible when he suggests that "O Canada" be that distinctive national anthem.
There are some people who are of the opinion that flags, anthems and symbols of that sort are unimportant or unnecessary. We do not agree with that opinion, Mr. Speaker. It is true that in the world of today we must build a world community and we must develop new loyalties to international institutions such as the United Nations and the British commonwealth of nations. However, in our view, there is no inconsistency between the development of new international loyalties and a sound sense of nationalism and national pride in Canada. It is our belief that symbols of nationalism such as a national flag and a national anthem increase sound national pride and a sense of unity which we most urgently need in Canada.
As we all know, Canada is approaching her one hundredth birthday which she will celebrate within a few years. We in this party believe that, before that one hundredth birthday, we should have all the reasonable symbols of adult nationhood, including a national flag, a national anthem and, may I add, a constitution made, passed and amendable within Canada.
In our view "O Canada" is the right selection because, as the hon. member has said, it is a great anthem. It is one which creates in those who sing a sense of pride, loyalty and of responsibility for Canada which we all need from one end of Canada to the other.
My riding, Mr. Speaker, is that of Greenwood. It used to be described as a riding in Tory Toronto. I imagine there was a day when the representatives from this riding, who were always Tories in the past, would have disapproved of this resolution. I wish to assure all members of this house-and thank God for it-that Tory Toronto is no longer Tory Toronto. Many people in the constituency were born in Great Britain, many of them either in Scotland or in England; and they retain their deep loyalty to the commonwealth and to the old country. They will continue to sing "God Save the Queen", not as a national anthem but as a symbol of the fact that we remain part of the commonwealth and loyal to the crown.

I was under the impression, probably erroneously, that Canadians of French extraction sing "O Canada" exactly the way we sing it but in the French language. I have heard it in the Polish and Ukrainian languages and they were exact translations, but this gives me an indication that those of French origin, when they sing it in French, have a different version of it and I would like to hear what the exact English translation of that would be.
If we want one national anthem it has got to be exact in one language, either English or French, which are the basic languages. We need not worry about the other ethnic groups because they will get proper translations. As I said before, people have strong feelings on this subject. If you can convince me that by putting this on the statute books it is not going to preclude or forbid the singing of other anthems-
Right.
If you can convince me it is going to give us greater unity-
Right.
-that it is going to give us greater loyalty-
Right.

But, sir, I believe we have that. Hon. members should go to our western towns where we have monuments to commemorate those who gave their lives for Canada. They will see Slavic, German, English, French and all kinds of names on them. Does not that indicate that we have unity? Was not our answer to the call in the last war an indication that we have unity?
I do not want to be accused of talking this motion out, although certainly I could do so if I wanted to, but in closing I wish to say that the house has more important matters to worry about to foster unity and to strengthen that Canadianism for which our boys fought and died, rather than squabble about which anthem we are going to sing, whether it is going to be "O Canada" or "Jeszeze Polska nie zginela."

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words in order to leave time for a vote. I want to put on the record something that some hon. members of the house may not be aware of, and which many members of the public may not know. I read from The Liberal Programme, which was a guide for us during the election campaign and outlined the goals and objectives of our party. Under the heading "Canadian Institutions" it reads:
Adopt a distinctively Canadian flag and anthem. Within two years of taking office, a new Liberal government will submit to parliament a design for a flag which cannot be mistaken for the emblem of any other country. When adopted, this will be the flag of Canada. "O Canada'' will be proclaimed our official anthem.
In the second paragraph under the heading "Maintain the honour given to traditional symbols" it goes on to say:
The union jack will be flown on appropriate occasions as a symbol of our membership in the commonwealth. A new Liberal government will also maintain the honour given to the traditional anthem which expresses Canada's devotion to the sovereign.
This is our objective and I might say that we were very close last night to having the opportunity of carrying out this program.
There is one thing in the motion which gives me cause for concern. It says that the English version is to be selected by the government. I would much prefer to see the English version of "O Canada" selected by parliament. In view of the speeches which members of the government have made on this subject I am not at all sure they should be trusted with the task of selecting the English version.

National Anthem
On rising to say a few words on this motion I wish to advise my hon. friends opposite that I am not going to talk it out.
Who is?

I don't know. The first comment I would like to make is that the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro) objected to the setting up of a committee, as was proposed in the speech from the throne, and hon. members opposite seem to have the feeling that setting up a committee accomplishes nothing. In reply I say committees do accomplish things and I am positive it is the firm intention of the government to set up a committee, well in advance of the hundredth anniversary of confederation, which will decide on a national anthem and national flag.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. member could let me ask him one brief question, to correct the record. The speech from the throne, I think, suggested a dominion-provincial conference, not a committee of this house.
How much more ridiculous could you get?
Two-flag Jack.

Mr. Speaker, I accept the question of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I did not suggest that a committee of this house was going to consider it, but I did suggest it was going to be submitted to a committee, or a conference, if that is the more correct word. The objection that I heard from the hon. member of the Social Credit group was that a committee, or a conference, would not accomplish what they wanted to do and that we ought today to settle this problem by a vote.
Right.

The hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Munro) was objecting to this method. If he will look back in the records of the late 1940's, I believe there was a committee set up in connection with our national symbols, the national anthem and the flag, and nothing was ever done in connection with the recommendations of that committee. It was found to be a very difficult problem; it is a very difficult problem. If the hon. member who introduced the resolution feels that the house ought to accept, in his words, the exact resolution he has put forward, I would suggest this would not be the proper way of approaching this matter. I believe it is a matter that ought to be settled in other ways, rather than by the wording that has been put into this resolution.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would permit me to ask him a factual question?
Certainly.

Did the hon. gentleman look up the records with respect to the committee in 1945 and 1946? I have not done so, but my recollection is that it was concerned exclusively with the flag and had nothing whatever to do with the national anthem, which is the exclusive subject of this motion. I admit that the flag question is a difficult one, but the question of a national anthem is not difficult at all. Everybody agrees it should be "O Canada".
Question.
Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say. 1 will-
Question.

-accept the statement of the hon. member. I have not today looked up the references to this subject. If that committee was concerned with the flag, I will accept the hon. member's statement. Regardless of that, it is the same general problem.
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

My question is this. Being somewhat interested in this subject I asked the government to answer this question: Has the government extended an invitation to the ten Canadian provinces to a consultation regarding the choice of a national flag and other national symbols? The answer I got was, no. I would ask my hon. friend to please tell me where that leaves his argument at the present time.
Up in the air.

In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I am not responsible for the actions of the government on this and they are not responsible for what I say. At this moment I am speaking as a private member and I have a few things to say that I would like to complete, if I may; otherwise I will break my word to the hon. gentlemen, whom I assured that I was not going to talk this out. There was recently a situation in the town of Barrie, in the province of Ontario, which is, as we know, predominantly English speaking. There was a situation in the school there. I am pointing out this situation merely to show that this problem and the feeling that has been sparked with regard to a national anthem is not confined merely to one province.
This was a situation where a number of high school students wrote to the Secretary

of State (Mr. Halpenny) and asked what was the national anthem. The Secretary of State replied that there was no Canadian national anthem. I am advised that there is no country in the world, except France, which has a national anthem by statute. But in any case, this question was asked and answered. Therefore, when they were asked to stand for the national anthem, for "God Save the Queen", they said, "This is not the national anthem" and refused to stand for the singing of "God Save the Queen". This is not a problem of one province. We all want a national anthem. I am certainly in general agreement with the-
Yes, walk out.
-principle-
Take "Pick" with you.

-of a national anthem, but the wording of the resolution does make it difficult in this country. There are two versions and I am advised that the one is not a translation of the other; they are very different.
I think that, so far as this resolution is concerned, if the French version is acceptable to those who sing it in French, and the English version is acceptable to those who sing it in English, there is no reason why that should not be accomplished. It is before six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I am going to resume my seat. I thank all the hon. members who assisted me in this speech, because I think incorporated in the interruptions were several hon. members who did not themselves want to get up and make their own speeches.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the hon. members who have been so vociferous in asking for a vote on this resolution have left the house, I imagine that they do not want their resolution voted on and I would therefore like to say a few words. I was very happy a few minutes ago to see the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) rise and state that there certainly is no argument about what our national anthem should be. I wish he had the same idea about our national flag, because I understand he supports two or three versions of it.
Six o'clock.

I, like the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Mandziuk), come from the west, where I was brought up in the tradition of singing "O Canada" at the commencement of proceedings and "God Save the Queen" at the end of proceedings. This served us very well. I personally would like to see "O Canada" adopted as our national anthem. However, there is in this resolution something that gives me some reservation about it,
